question: What is the purpose of an alcohol evaporator found on some air brake systems?
choice_a: To cool the compressor during hot weather
choice_b: To reduce the risk of ice in air brake valves and other parts during cold weather
choice_c: To replace the need for daily air tank drainage
choice_d: To increase the compressor cut-out pressure
explanation: Some air brake systems have an alcohol evaporator to put alcohol into the air system, which helps reduce the risk of ice in air brake valves and other parts during cold weather, since ice inside the system can make the brakes stop working.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 5, Air Brakes, Subsection 5.1.5, Alcohol Evaporator

question: If a vehicle has an alcohol evaporator, is daily air tank drainage still necessary during cold weather?
choice_a: No, the evaporator makes tank drainage unnecessary
choice_b: No, but only if the vehicle was built after 1994
choice_c: Only if the alcohol container is empty
choice_d: Yes, daily air tank drainage is still needed to get rid of water and oil, unless the system has automatic drain valves
explanation: The manual states that daily air tank drainage is still needed to get rid of water and oil, unless the system has automatic drain valves, even when an alcohol evaporator is present.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 5, Air Brakes, Subsection 5.1.5, Alcohol Evaporator

question: Where is the safety relief valve installed in an air brake system?
choice_a: In the last tank before the brake chambers
choice_b: In the first tank the air compressor pumps air to
choice_c: In the alcohol evaporator container
choice_d: In the brake pedal assembly
explanation: A safety relief valve is installed in the first tank the air compressor pumps air to, protecting the tank and the rest of the system from too much pressure.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 5, Air Brakes, Subsection 5.1.6, Safety Valve

question: The safety relief valve is usually set to open at about what pressure?
choice_a: 100 psi
choice_b: 175 psi
choice_c: 125 psi
choice_d: 150 psi
explanation: The valve is usually set to open at 150 psi; if the safety valve releases air, something is wrong and the fault should be fixed by a mechanic.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 5, Air Brakes, Subsection 5.1.6, Safety Valve

question: What should a driver do if the safety relief valve releases air?
choice_a: Add more alcohol to the evaporator
choice_b: Recognize that something is wrong and have the fault fixed by a mechanic
choice_c: Manually reset the wig wag arm
choice_d: Ignore it, this is normal during hard braking
explanation: If the safety valve releases air, something is wrong, and the fault should be fixed by a mechanic.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 5, Air Brakes, Subsection 5.1.6, Safety Valve

question: What are two other names the manual gives for the air brake pedal?
choice_a: The trolley valve or hand valve
choice_b: The foot valve or treadle valve
choice_c: The modulating valve or wig wag
choice_d: The governor or power screw
explanation: The brake pedal is also called the foot valve or treadle valve.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 5, Air Brakes, Subsection 5.1.7, The Brake Pedal

question: What happens to air pressure in the tanks when a driver releases the brake pedal?
choice_a: It stays exactly the same
choice_b: The safety valve opens automatically
choice_c: Compressed air goes out of the system, reducing tank pressure, which must be made up by the compressor
choice_d: It increases automatically
explanation: Releasing the brakes lets some compressed air go out of the system, so the air pressure in the tanks is reduced, and it must be made up by the air compressor.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 5, Air Brakes, Subsection 5.1.7, The Brake Pedal

question: What can happen if a driver presses and releases the brake pedal unnecessarily and repeatedly?
choice_a: It triggers the ABS malfunction lamp
choice_b: It can let air out of the system faster than the compressor can replace it, and if pressure gets too low the brakes won't work
choice_c: It sharpens brake response with no downside
choice_d: It automatically engages the front brake limiting valve
explanation: Pressing and releasing the pedal unnecessarily can let air out faster than the compressor can replace it; if the pressure gets too low, the brakes won't work.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 5, Air Brakes, Subsection 5.1.7, The Brake Pedal

question: What is the most common type of foundation brake used at each wheel?
choice_a: The wedge brake
choice_b: The disc brake
choice_c: The s-cam drum brake
choice_d: The modulating brake
explanation: Foundation brakes are used at each wheel, and the most common type is the s-cam drum brake.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 5, Air Brakes, Subsection 5.1.8, Foundation Brakes

topic: Foundation Brakes - Brake Drums, Shoes, and Linings
question: What causes the heat that is created when a drum brake stops a vehicle?
choice_a: The alcohol evaporator
choice_b: The air compressor motor
choice_c: Friction created when the brake shoes and linings are pushed against the inside of the drum
choice_d: The safety relief valve releasing air
explanation: To stop, the brake shoes and linings are pushed against the inside of the drum, which causes friction that slows the vehicle and creates heat.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 5, Air Brakes, Subsection 5.1.8, Foundation Brakes, Brake Drums, Shoes, and Linings

topic: Foundation Brakes - Brake Drums, Shoes, and Linings
question: What determines how much heat a brake drum can take without being damaged?
choice_a: The setting of the front brake limiting valve
choice_b: How hard and how long the brakes are used
choice_c: The number of brake chambers on the axle
choice_d: The color of the drum
explanation: The heat a drum can take without damage depends on how hard and how long the brakes are used, and too much heat can make the brakes stop working.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 5, Air Brakes, Subsection 5.1.8, Foundation Brakes, Brake Drums, Shoes, and Linings

question: In an s-cam brake, what happens after the driver pushes the brake pedal and air enters the brake chamber?
choice_a: A power screw clamps the disc between brake lining pads
choice_b: A wedge is pushed directly between the ends of two brake shoes
choice_c: Hydraulic fluid pushes a caliper closed
choice_d: Air pressure pushes the rod out, moving the slack adjuster and twisting the brake camshaft, which turns the s-cam and forces the shoes against the drum
explanation: Air pressure pushes the rod out, moving the slack adjuster and twisting the brake camshaft; this turns the s-cam, which forces the brake shoes away from one another and presses them against the inside of the brake drum.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 5, Air Brakes, Subsection 5.1.8, Foundation Brakes, S-cam Brakes

question: Why is the s-cam called an "s-cam"?
choice_a: Because it is shaped like the letter "S"
choice_b: Because it only spins in one direction
choice_c: Because it was invented by a company named S-Cam Inc.
choice_d: Because it stands for "safety cam"
explanation: The s-cam is so called because it is shaped like the letter "S."
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 5, Air Brakes, Subsection 5.1.8, Foundation Brakes, S-cam Brakes

question: What happens to the wheels when a driver releases the brake pedal on an s-cam brake system?
choice_a: The s-cam rotates back and a spring pulls the brake shoes away from the drum, letting the wheels roll freely
choice_b: The power screw continues to clamp the disc
choice_c: The parking brake automatically engages
choice_d: The wedge locks the shoes in place permanently
explanation: When you release the brake pedal, the s-cam rotates back and a spring pulls the brake shoes away from the drum, letting the wheels roll freely again.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 5, Air Brakes, Subsection 5.1.8, Foundation Brakes, S-cam Brakes

question: In wedge brakes, how does the brake chamber push rod act on the brake shoes?
choice_a: It rotates a power screw against a rotor
choice_b: It twists a camshaft to turn an s-cam
choice_c: It pushes a wedge directly between the ends of two brake shoes, shoving them apart and against the inside of the brake drum
choice_d: It releases hydraulic fluid into a caliper
explanation: In wedge brakes, the brake chamber push rod pushes a wedge directly between the ends of two brake shoes, shoving them apart and against the inside of the brake drum.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 5, Air Brakes, Subsection 5.1.8, Foundation Brakes, Wedge Brakes

question: According to the manual, wedge type brakes may be configured in which of the following ways?
choice_a: Only with a single brake chamber and only self-adjusting
choice_b: Only on trailers, never on tractors
choice_c: Only with hydraulic calipers
choice_d: With a single brake chamber or two brake chambers, and may be self-adjusting or require manual adjustment
explanation: Wedge brakes may have a single brake chamber, or two brake chambers pushing wedges in at both ends of the brake shoes, and wedge type brakes may be self-adjusting or may require manual adjustment.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 5, Air Brakes, Subsection 5.1.8, Foundation Brakes, Wedge Brakes

question: In air-operated disc brakes, what part is used instead of the s-cam?
choice_a: A power screw
choice_b: A hydraulic piston
choice_c: A wedge
choice_d: A modulating valve
explanation: In air-operated disc brakes, instead of the s-cam, a "power screw" is used; the pressure of the brake chamber on the slack adjuster turns the power screw.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 5, Air Brakes, Subsection 5.1.8, Foundation Brakes, Disc Brakes

question: The manual compares the clamping action of an air-operated disc brake's power screw and caliper to what everyday tool?
choice_a: A vise grip
choice_b: A hydraulic jack
choice_c: A pair of pliers
choice_d: A large c-clamp
explanation: The power screw clamps the disc or rotor between the brake lining pads of a caliper, similar to a large c-clamp.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 5, Air Brakes, Subsection 5.1.8, Foundation Brakes, Disc Brakes

question: Compared to s-cam brakes, how common are wedge brakes and disc brakes?
choice_a: They are less common than s-cam brakes
choice_b: They are more common than s-cam brakes
choice_c: They are equally common
choice_d: Disc brakes are more common but wedge brakes are rare
explanation: The manual states that wedge brakes and disc brakes are less common than s-cam brakes.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 5, Air Brakes, Subsection 5.1.8, Foundation Brakes

question: What does the supply pressure gauge on a vehicle with air brakes tell the driver?
choice_a: How fast the compressor is cycling
choice_b: How much air pressure is currently being applied to the brakes
choice_c: The temperature of the brake drums
choice_d: How much pressure is in the air tanks
explanation: All vehicles with air brakes have a pressure gauge connected to the air tank, and these gauges tell you how much pressure is in the air tanks.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 5, Air Brakes, Subsection 5.1.9, Supply Pressure Gauges

question: How does a vehicle with a dual air brake system typically display supply pressure?
choice_a: A single needle switches between systems every few seconds
choice_b: There is no gauge required for dual systems
choice_c: There is a gauge for each half of the system, or a single gauge with two needles
choice_d: Only the primary system gets a gauge
explanation: If the vehicle has a dual air brake system, there will be a gauge for each half of the system, or a single gauge with two needles.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 5, Air Brakes, Subsection 5.1.9, Supply Pressure Gauges

question: What does the application pressure gauge show, and is it found on every vehicle?
choice_a: It shows tank pressure and is on every vehicle
choice_b: It shows spring brake status and is only on buses
choice_c: It shows how much air pressure you are applying to the brakes, and it is not on all vehicles
choice_d: It shows engine RPM and is required on all vehicles
explanation: The application pressure gauge shows how much air pressure you are applying to the brakes; the manual notes this gauge is not on all vehicles.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 5, Air Brakes, Subsection 5.1.10, Application Pressure Gauge

question: What does it mean if a driver has to increase application pressure to hold the same speed?
choice_a: The safety valve has opened
choice_b: The brakes are fading, and the driver should slow down and use a lower gear
choice_c: The parking brake is partially engaged
choice_d: The tires need more air
explanation: Increasing application pressure to hold the same speed means the brakes are fading; the driver should slow down and use a lower gear, and this can also be caused by brakes out of adjustment, air leaks, or mechanical problems.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 5, Air Brakes, Subsection 5.1.10, Application Pressure Gauge

question: A visible low air pressure warning signal must come on before the air pressure in the tanks falls below what level?
choice_a: 55 psi
choice_b: 100 psi
choice_c: 35 psi
choice_d: 45 psi
explanation: A warning signal you can see must come on before the air pressure in the tanks falls below 55 psi (or one half the compressor governor cutout pressure on older vehicles).
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 5, Air Brakes, Subsection 5.1.11, Low Air Pressure Warning

question: On older vehicles, the low air pressure warning threshold may instead be set at what level?
choice_a: 10 psi above cut-in pressure
choice_b: One half the compressor governor cutout pressure
choice_c: Double the compressor governor cutout pressure
choice_d: The exact same pressure as the safety valve setting
explanation: The manual states the warning must come on before pressure falls below 55 psi, or one half the compressor governor cutout pressure on older vehicles.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 5, Air Brakes, Subsection 5.1.11, Low Air Pressure Warning

question: What form does the low air pressure warning usually take?
choice_a: A vibration in the steering wheel
choice_b: An automatic reduction in engine speed
choice_c: A green light only
choice_d: A red light, and a buzzer may also come on
explanation: The warning is usually a red light, and a buzzer may also come on.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 5, Air Brakes, Subsection 5.1.11, Low Air Pressure Warning

topic: Low Air Pressure Warning - Wig Wag
question: What is a "wig wag" warning device?
choice_a: A valve that automatically drains the tanks
choice_b: A dashboard light that flashes only above 40 mph
choice_c: A device that drops a mechanical arm into the driver's view when system pressure drops below 55 psi
choice_d: A buzzer that only activates the parking brake
explanation: The wig wag device drops a mechanical arm into your view when the pressure in the system drops below 55 psi.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 5, Air Brakes, Subsection 5.1.11, Low Air Pressure Warning

topic: Low Air Pressure Warning - Wig Wag
question: How does a manual reset wig wag differ from an automatic wig wag?
choice_a: The manual reset type only works on buses
choice_b: The manual reset type resets itself automatically at 100 psi
choice_c: The manual reset type must be placed in the "out of view" position by hand, and will not stay in place until pressure is above 55 psi
choice_d: There is no difference between them
explanation: An automatic wig wag will rise out of view when pressure rises above 55 psi, but the manual reset type must be placed in the "out of view" position manually, and it will not stay in place until the pressure in the system is above 55 psi.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 5, Air Brakes, Subsection 5.1.11, Low Air Pressure Warning

question: On large buses, it is common for the low pressure warning devices to signal at what pressure range?
explanation: On large buses it is common for the low pressure warning devices to signal at 80-85 psi.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 5, Air Brakes, Subsection 5.1.11, Low Air Pressure Warning

question: How does the air brake system turn on the brake lights when a driver applies the brakes?
choice_a: With a mechanical cable connected to the pedal
choice_b: With an electric switch that works by air pressure
choice_c: The ABS computer triggers the lights
choice_d: The governor sends a signal to the lights
explanation: The air brake system uses an electric switch that works by air pressure; the switch turns on the brake lights when you put on the air brakes.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 5, Air Brakes, Subsection 5.1.12, Stop Light Switch

question: What type of vehicles were equipped with a front brake limiting valve and cab control?
choice_a: Only vehicles equipped with ABS
choice_b: Only vehicles built after 1997
choice_c: Only buses
choice_d: Some older vehicles made before 1975
explanation: Some older vehicles (made before 1975) have a front brake limiting valve and a control in the cab, usually marked "normal" and "slippery."
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 5, Air Brakes, Subsection 5.1.13, Front Brake Limiting Valve

question: What happens to front brake pressure when the front brake limiting valve control is placed in the "slippery" position?
choice_a: It cuts the normal air pressure to the front brakes by half
choice_b: It has no effect on pressure, only on the warning light
choice_c: It doubles the normal air pressure to the front brakes
choice_d: It shuts off the front brakes entirely
explanation: In the "slippery" position, the limiting valve cuts the "normal" air pressure to the front brakes by half.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 5, Air Brakes, Subsection 5.1.13, Front Brake Limiting Valve

question: According to the manual, is front wheel braking good under all conditions, including on ice?
choice_a: No, front wheel skids are common on ice, so the limiting valve should stay in "slippery"
choice_b: Front brakes should never be used below 20 mph
choice_c: Limiting valves improve stopping power in all conditions
choice_d: Yes, tests have shown front wheel skids from braking are not likely even on ice, and the control should be kept in "normal"
explanation: Front wheel braking is good under all conditions; tests have shown front wheel skids from braking are not likely even on ice, so the control should be in the "normal" position for normal stopping power, since limiting valves actually reduce the stopping power of the vehicle.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 5, Air Brakes, Subsection 5.1.13, Front Brake Limiting Valve

question: Automatic front wheel limiting valves reduce air to the front brakes except when the brakes are applied very hard, meaning at what application pressure or more?
choice_a: 55 psi
choice_b: 20 psi
choice_c: 100 psi
choice_d: 45 psi
explanation: Many vehicles have automatic front wheel limiting valves that reduce air to the front brakes except when the brakes are put on very hard, at 55 psi or more application pressure; these valves cannot be controlled by the driver.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 5, Air Brakes, Subsection 5.1.13, Front Brake Limiting Valve

question: Why must emergency and parking brakes be held on by mechanical force rather than air pressure alone?
choice_a: Because federal law bans air-held parking brakes
choice_b: Because air pressure can eventually leak away
choice_c: Because mechanical force responds faster to the pedal
choice_d: Because mechanical force is cheaper to produce
explanation: All trucks, truck tractors, and buses must be equipped with emergency brakes and parking brakes, which must be held on by mechanical force because air pressure can eventually leak away; spring brakes are usually used to meet these needs.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 5, Air Brakes, Subsection 5.1.14, Spring Brakes

question: How do spring brakes work while a vehicle is being driven?
choice_a: Powerful springs are held back by air pressure; if the air pressure is removed, the springs put on the brakes
choice_b: Springs are disconnected entirely while the vehicle moves
choice_c: Springs only engage when the ABS malfunction lamp is lit
choice_d: Springs are held back by hydraulic fluid
explanation: When driving, powerful springs are held back by air pressure; if the air pressure is removed, the springs put on the brakes.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 5, Air Brakes, Subsection 5.1.14, Spring Brakes

question: What happens when the driver uses the parking brake control to let air out of the spring brakes?
choice_a: The safety valve opens
choice_b: The springs put on the brakes
choice_c: The wig wag arm drops into view
choice_d: The service brakes are permanently disabled
explanation: A parking brake control in the cab allows the driver to let the air out of the spring brakes, and this lets the springs put the brakes on.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 5, Air Brakes, Subsection 5.1.14, Spring Brakes

question: What happens to the spring brakes if a leak in the air brake system causes all the air to be lost?
choice_a: Only the front spring brakes activate
choice_b: The springs will also cause the brakes to come on
choice_c: The spring brakes remain fully released
choice_d: The vehicle will coast with no braking at all
explanation: A leak in the air brake system, which causes all the air to be lost, will also cause the springs to put on the brakes.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 5, Air Brakes, Subsection 5.1.14, Spring Brakes

question: On a tractor or straight truck, spring brakes will come fully on when air pressure drops into approximately what range?
choice_a: 10 to 15 psi
choice_b: 55 to 65 psi
choice_c: 20 to 45 psi (typically 20 to 30 psi)
choice_d: 100 to 125 psi
explanation: Tractor and straight truck spring brakes will come fully on when air pressure drops to a range of 20 to 45 psi, typically 20 to 30 psi.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 5, Air Brakes, Subsection 5.1.14, Spring Brakes

question: What should a driver do when the low air pressure warning light and buzzer first come on?
choice_a: Increase speed to reach the nearest repair shop
choice_b: Wait for the spring brakes to come on automatically before stopping
choice_c: Bring the vehicle to a safe stop right away, while you can still control the brakes
choice_d: Turn off the electrical system to save power
explanation: Do not wait for the brakes to come on automatically; when the low air pressure warning light and buzzer first come on, bring the vehicle to a safe stop right away, while you can still control the brakes.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 5, Air Brakes, Subsection 5.1.14, Spring Brakes

question: What does the braking power of spring brakes depend on?
choice_a: The color of the parking brake knob
choice_b: The vehicle's model year only
choice_c: The alcohol evaporator being full
choice_d: The brakes being in adjustment
explanation: The braking power of spring brakes depends on the brakes being in adjustment; if the brakes are not adjusted properly, neither the regular brakes nor the emergency/parking brakes will work right.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 5, Air Brakes, Subsection 5.1.14, Spring Brakes

question: On newer vehicles with air brakes, how does the driver apply the parking (spring) brakes?
choice_a: By pulling out a diamond-shaped, yellow, push-pull control knob
choice_b: By pressing the brake pedal all the way to the floor
choice_c: By pushing in a round blue knob
choice_d: By flipping the modulating control lever to the left
explanation: In newer vehicles with air brakes, you put on the parking brakes using a diamond-shaped, yellow, push-pull control knob; you pull the knob out to apply the parking brakes and push it in to release them.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 5, Air Brakes, Subsection 5.1.15, Parking Brake Controls

question: Why does the manual caution drivers never to push the brake pedal down when the spring brakes are on?
choice_a: The brakes could be damaged by the combined forces of the springs and the air pressure
choice_b: It automatically drains the air tanks
choice_c: It will disable the ABS system permanently
choice_d: It has no effect and is just an old habit to avoid
explanation: If you push the brake pedal down when the spring brakes are on, the brakes could be damaged by the combined forces of the springs and the air pressure; many systems are designed to prevent this, but not all, so it is best to develop the habit of not doing it.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 5, Air Brakes, Subsection 5.1.15, Parking Brake Controls

topic: Parking Brake Controls - Modulating Control Valves
question: What is a modulating control valve used for on some vehicles?
choice_a: To reset the wig wag warning arm
choice_b: To control the alcohol evaporator temperature
choice_c: To switch between the primary and secondary air systems
choice_d: To apply the spring brakes gradually using a dashboard control handle
explanation: A modulating valve is a control handle on the dash board that may be used to apply the spring brakes gradually; it is spring-loaded so the driver has a feel for the braking action, and the more the control lever is moved, the harder the spring brakes come on.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 5, Air Brakes, Subsection 5.1.15, Parking Brake Controls, Modulating Control Valves

topic: Parking Brake Controls - Modulating Control Valves
question: When parking a vehicle equipped with a modulating control valve, what should the driver do with the lever?
choice_a: Push it in halfway and release it
choice_b: Move it as far as it will go and hold it in place with the locking device
choice_c: Remove it entirely
choice_d: Leave it in the neutral position
explanation: When parking a vehicle with a modulating control valve, move the lever as far as it will go and hold it in place with the locking device.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 5, Air Brakes, Subsection 5.1.15, Parking Brake Controls, Modulating Control Valves

topic: Parking Brake Controls - Dual Parking Control Valves
question: Why do some vehicles, such as buses, have a separate air tank connected to a dual parking control valve system?
choice_a: To operate the ABS malfunction lamp
choice_b: So the driver can release the spring brakes to move the vehicle in an emergency after main air pressure is lost
choice_c: To power the air conditioning
choice_d: To supply air to the alcohol evaporator
explanation: When main air pressure is lost, the spring brakes come on; some vehicles have a separate air tank that can be used to release the spring brakes so the driver can move the vehicle in an emergency.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 5, Air Brakes, Subsection 5.1.15, Parking Brake Controls, Dual Parking Control Valves

topic: Parking Brake Controls - Dual Parking Control Valves
question: In the dual parking control valve system, why must a driver plan carefully when moving the vehicle using the separate air supply?
choice_a: Because using it disables the primary air system permanently
choice_b: Because the separate tank powers the entire vehicle indefinitely
choice_c: Because it can only be used once per day
choice_d: Because there is only enough air in the separate tank to release the spring brakes a few times
explanation: There is only enough air in the separate tank to release the spring brakes a few times, so the driver should plan carefully, or risk being stopped in a dangerous location when the separate air supply runs out.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 5, Air Brakes, Subsection 5.1.15, Parking Brake Controls, Dual Parking Control Valves

question: Truck tractors with air brakes built on or after what date are required to be equipped with antilock brakes?
choice_a: January 1, 2000
choice_b: March 1, 1997
choice_c: March 1, 1998
choice_d: March 1, 1995
explanation: Truck tractors with air brakes built on or after March 1, 1997, are required to be equipped with antilock brakes.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 5, Air Brakes, Subsection 5.1.16, Antilock Braking Systems (ABS)

question: Other air brake vehicles -- trucks, buses, trailers, and converter dollies -- are required to have ABS if built on or after what date?
choice_a: March 1, 1997
choice_b: March 1, 1999
choice_c: January 1, 2000
choice_d: March 1, 1998
explanation: Other air brake vehicles (trucks, buses, trailers, and converter dollies) built on or after March 1, 1998, are required to be equipped with antilock brakes.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 5, Air Brakes, Subsection 5.1.16, Antilock Braking Systems (ABS)

question: How can a driver determine whether a vehicle built before the ABS requirement dates has been voluntarily equipped with ABS?
choice_a: There is no way to tell
choice_b: By checking the certification label for the date of manufacture
choice_c: By testing the front brake limiting valve
choice_d: By checking the alcohol evaporator level
explanation: Many commercial vehicles built before the ABS-required dates have been voluntarily equipped with ABS; the driver should check the certification label for the date of manufacture to determine if the vehicle is equipped with ABS.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 5, Air Brakes, Subsection 5.1.16, Antilock Braking Systems (ABS)

question: What is ABS, according to the manual?
choice_a: A mechanical device that shortens stopping distance by half
choice_b: A device that increases spring brake pressure
choice_c: A backup hydraulic braking system
choice_d: A computerized system that keeps your wheels from locking up during hard brake applications
explanation: ABS is a computerized system that keeps your wheels from locking up during hard brake applications.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 5, Air Brakes, Subsection 5.1.16, Antilock Braking Systems (ABS)

question: What color are the ABS malfunction lamps on tractors, trucks, and buses?
choice_a: Yellow
choice_b: Green
choice_c: Blue
choice_d: Red
explanation: Vehicles with ABS have yellow malfunction lamps; tractors, trucks, and buses will have yellow ABS malfunction lamps on the instrument panel.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 5, Air Brakes, Subsection 5.1.16, Antilock Braking Systems (ABS)

question: Where are the yellow ABS malfunction lamps located on trailers?
choice_a: Trailers are never required to have ABS lamps
choice_b: On the left side, either on the front or rear corner
choice_c: On the right side only, near the taillight
choice_d: On the instrument panel inside the cab
explanation: Trailers will have yellow ABS malfunction lamps on the left side, either on the front or rear corner.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 5, Air Brakes, Subsection 5.1.16, Antilock Braking Systems (ABS)

question: Dollies manufactured on or after March 1, 1998 are required to have an ABS lamp located where?
choice_a: On the right side
choice_b: On the left side
choice_c: On top of the dolly
choice_d: Inside the towing vehicle's cab only
explanation: Dollies manufactured on or after March 1, 1998 are required to have a lamp on the left side.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 5, Air Brakes, Subsection 5.1.16, Antilock Braking Systems (ABS)

question: How does the ABS malfunction lamp typically behave at start-up on newer vehicles?
choice_a: It stays on for the entire trip
choice_b: It flashes continuously until 55 mph is reached
choice_c: It never comes on until a malfunction occurs
choice_d: It comes on for a bulb check and then goes out quickly
explanation: On newer vehicles, the malfunction lamp comes on at start-up for a bulb check, and then goes out quickly.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 5, Air Brakes, Subsection 5.1.16, Antilock Braking Systems (ABS)

question: On older ABS systems, how long could the malfunction lamp stay on after start-up?
choice_a: It could stay on until you are driving over five mph
choice_b: It never turns off until serviced
choice_c: Until the parking brake is released
choice_d: Exactly ten seconds
explanation: On older systems, the lamp could stay on until you are driving over five mph.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 5, Air Brakes, Subsection 5.1.16, Antilock Braking Systems (ABS)

question: What does it mean if the ABS malfunction lamp stays on after the bulb check, or comes on once the vehicle is under way?
choice_a: The driver may have lost ABS control at one or more wheels
choice_b: It simply means the headlights are on
choice_c: The parking brake has been engaged
choice_d: The service brakes have failed completely
explanation: If the lamp stays on after the bulb check, or goes on once you are under way, you may have lost ABS control at one or more wheels.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 5, Air Brakes, Subsection 5.1.16, Antilock Braking Systems (ABS)

question: For towed units manufactured before ABS was required, how can a driver tell if the unit is equipped with ABS?
choice_a: By looking under the vehicle for the electronic control unit (ECU) and wheel speed sensor wires coming from the back of the brakes
choice_b: There is no way to determine this
choice_c: By checking the alcohol evaporator
choice_d: By testing the front brake limiting valve
explanation: It may be difficult to tell if a towed unit made before ABS was required is equipped with it; the driver should look under the vehicle for the electronic control unit (ECU) and wheel speed sensor wires coming from the back of the brakes.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 5, Air Brakes, Subsection 5.1.16, Antilock Braking Systems (ABS)

question: Does ABS decrease or increase a vehicle's normal braking capability?
choice_a: It replaces the need for normal service brakes
choice_b: ABS is an addition to normal brakes and does not decrease or increase normal braking capability; it only activates when wheels are about to lock up
choice_c: It significantly increases normal braking capability at all times
choice_d: It decreases normal braking capability to prevent skids
explanation: ABS is an addition to your normal brakes; it does not decrease or increase your normal braking capability, and ABS only activates when wheels are about to lock up.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 5, Air Brakes, Subsection 5.1.16, Antilock Braking Systems (ABS)

question: Does ABS necessarily shorten a vehicle's stopping distance?
choice_a: Yes, but only on wet pavement
choice_b: No, ABS has no effect on braking whatsoever
choice_c: Yes, ABS always cuts stopping distance in half
choice_d: No, ABS does not necessarily shorten stopping distance, but it does help you keep the vehicle under control during hard braking
explanation: ABS does not necessarily shorten your stopping distance, but it does help you keep the vehicle under control during hard braking.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 5, Air Brakes, Subsection 5.1.16, Antilock Braking Systems (ABS)

question: What is a dual air brake system?
choice_a: A system with two brake pedals for the driver and a passenger
choice_b: Two separate air brake systems that use a single set of brake controls, each with its own tanks, hoses, and lines
choice_c: A system found only on buses
choice_d: A system combining hydraulic and air brakes on the same axle
explanation: A dual air brake system has two separate air brake systems, which use a single set of brake controls; each system has its own air tanks, hoses, lines, etc.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 5, Air Brakes, Section 5.2, Dual Air Brake

question: In a dual air brake system, what are the two separate systems called, and which axles do they typically operate?
choice_a: The "upper" system operates the trailer; the "lower" system operates the tractor
choice_b: The "primary" system typically operates the rear axle(s); the "secondary" system typically operates the front axle
choice_c: The "main" system operates all axles; the "auxiliary" system is a backup only
choice_d: Both systems are called "primary" and operate identical axles for redundancy
explanation: One system typically operates the regular brakes on the rear axle or axles and is called the "primary" system; the other operates the regular brakes on the front axle and is called the "secondary" system.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 5, Air Brakes, Section 5.2, Dual Air Brake

question: In a dual air brake system, do both the primary and secondary systems supply air to the trailer, if there is one?
choice_a: No, only the primary system supplies the trailer
choice_b: No, only the secondary system supplies the trailer
choice_c: Yes, both systems supply air to the trailer, if there is one
choice_d: Trailers never receive air from either system
explanation: Both systems supply air to the trailer (if there is one).
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 5, Air Brakes, Section 5.2, Dual Air Brake

question: Before driving a vehicle with a dual air system, the compressor should build up a minimum of what pressure in both the primary and secondary systems?
choice_a: 100 psi
choice_b: 75 psi
choice_c: 125 psi
choice_d: 55 psi
explanation: Before driving a vehicle with a dual air system, allow time for the air compressor to build up a minimum of 100 psi pressure in both the primary and secondary systems.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 5, Air Brakes, Section 5.2, Dual Air Brake

question: At what pressure should the low air pressure warning light and buzzer shut off as air pressure rises in a dual air system?
choice_a: At exactly 55 psi
choice_b: At exactly 100 psi
choice_c: At a value set by the manufacturer that must be greater than 55 psi
choice_d: At exactly 150 psi
explanation: The warning light and buzzer should shut off when air pressure in both systems rises to a value set by the manufacturer, and this value must be greater than 55 psi.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 5, Air Brakes, Section 5.2, Dual Air Brake

question: What should a driver do if the low air pressure warning light and buzzer come on while driving a dual air system vehicle?
choice_a: Stop right away and safely park the vehicle, then have the air brake system fixed
choice_b: Switch immediately to the parking brake control for all future stops
choice_c: Only worry if both systems drop below 20 psi
choice_d: Continue driving normally since the other system compensates fully
explanation: The warning light and buzzer should come on before pressure drops below 55 psi in either system; if this happens while driving, the driver should stop right away and safely park the vehicle, and have the air brake system fixed.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 5, Air Brakes, Section 5.2, Dual Air Brake

question: What happens if one air system in a dual air brake vehicle becomes very low on pressure?
choice_a: Either the front or the rear brakes will not be operating fully, meaning it will take longer to stop
choice_b: The vehicle automatically shifts to neutral
choice_c: Nothing changes because the other system fully compensates
choice_d: The spring brakes are permanently disabled
explanation: If one air system is very low on pressure, either the front or the rear brakes will not be operating fully, which means it will take longer to stop.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 5, Air Brakes, Section 5.2, Dual Air Brake

question: During the Step 2 engine compartment check, what should a driver check on a belt-driven air compressor?
choice_a: The compressor oil color only
choice_b: The ABS malfunction lamp
choice_c: The alcohol evaporator fluid level only
choice_d: The condition and tightness of the drive belt
explanation: If the air compressor is belt-driven, check the condition and tightness of the belt; it should be in good condition.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 5, Air Brakes, Subsection 5.3.1, During Step 2 Engine Compartment Checks

topic: Inspecting Air Brake Systems - Slack Adjusters
question: How should a driver check the slack adjusters on s-cam brakes during a walk-around inspection?
choice_a: Park on level ground, chock the wheels, release the parking brakes, and pull hard on each reachable slack adjuster with gloves
choice_b: Check only the manufacturer's paperwork
choice_c: Apply the parking brakes fully and inspect visually only
choice_d: Drive the vehicle at 20 mph and listen for noise
explanation: Park on level ground and chock the wheels to prevent the vehicle from moving, release the parking brakes so you can move the slack adjusters, use gloves, and pull hard on each slack adjuster that you can reach.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 5, Air Brakes, Subsection 5.3.2, Walk-around Inspection, Slack Adjusters

topic: Inspecting Air Brake Systems - Slack Adjusters
question: If a slack adjuster moves more than about how far, where the push rod attaches to it, does it probably need adjustment?
choice_a: About one-half inch
choice_b: About one inch
choice_c: About one-quarter inch
choice_d: About three inches
explanation: If a slack adjuster moves more than about one inch where the push rod attaches to it, it probably needs adjustment; vehicles with too much brake slack can be very hard to stop.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 5, Air Brakes, Subsection 5.3.2, Walk-around Inspection, Slack Adjusters

topic: Inspecting Air Brake Systems - Slack Adjusters
question: What does the manual identify as the most common problem found in roadside inspections?
choice_a: Out-of-adjustment brakes
choice_b: Missing mud flaps
choice_c: A dirty windshield
choice_d: A malfunctioning alcohol evaporator
explanation: Out-of-adjustment brakes are the most common problem found in roadside inspections, so drivers should be safe and check the slack adjusters.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 5, Air Brakes, Subsection 5.3.2, Walk-around Inspection, Slack Adjusters

topic: Inspecting Air Brake Systems - Automatic Slack Adjusters
question: Since what year have all vehicles been built with automatic slack adjusters?
explanation: All vehicles built since 1994 have automatic slack adjustors.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 5, Air Brakes, Subsection 5.3.2, Walk-around Inspection, Slack Adjusters

topic: Inspecting Air Brake Systems - Automatic Slack Adjusters
question: Even though automatic slack adjusters adjust themselves during full brake applications, what must the driver still do?
choice_a: Manually adjust them daily
choice_b: Replace them every 90 days regardless of condition
choice_c: Nothing, they never need checking
choice_d: They must still be checked
explanation: Even though automatic slack adjustors adjust themselves during full brake applications, they must be checked.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 5, Air Brakes, Subsection 5.3.2, Walk-around Inspection, Slack Adjusters

topic: Inspecting Air Brake Systems - Automatic Slack Adjusters
question: In a vehicle with automatic adjusters, what does it indicate when the pushrod stroke exceeds the legal brake adjustment limit?
choice_a: The vehicle needs a new alcohol evaporator
choice_b: The front brake limiting valve needs replacement
choice_c: This is completely normal and requires no action
choice_d: A mechanical problem exists in the adjuster itself, a problem with related foundation brake components, or the adjuster was improperly installed
explanation: When the pushrod stroke exceeds the legal brake adjustment limit on a vehicle with automatic adjusters, it indicates a mechanical problem in the adjuster itself, a problem with the related foundation brake components, or that the adjuster was improperly installed.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 5, Air Brakes, Subsection 5.3.2, Walk-around Inspection, Slack Adjusters

topic: Inspecting Air Brake Systems - Automatic Slack Adjusters
question: Why does the manual warn against routinely manually adjusting an automatic slack adjuster to bring it within legal limits?
choice_a: It has no real downside
choice_b: It generally masks a mechanical problem rather than fixing it, and can give a false sense of security about brake effectiveness
choice_c: It voids the manufacturer's warranty in every case
choice_d: It is illegal in all circumstances, even emergencies
explanation: The manual adjustment of an automatic adjuster is generally masking a mechanical problem and not fixing it; it is recommended that the vehicle be taken to a repair facility as soon as possible, since manual adjustment may give a driver a false sense of security regarding the effectiveness of the braking system.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 5, Air Brakes, Subsection 5.3.2, Walk-around Inspection, Slack Adjusters

topic: Inspecting Air Brake Systems - Automatic Slack Adjusters
question: According to the manual, when should the manual adjustment of an automatic slack adjuster be used?
choice_a: Only on vehicles built before 1994
choice_b: Only as a temporary measure to correct adjustment in an emergency situation, since it is likely the brake will soon be out of adjustment again
choice_c: Never, under any circumstances
choice_d: As a routine weekly maintenance step
explanation: The manual adjustment of an automatic adjuster should only be used as a temporary measure to correct the adjustment in an emergency situation, as it is likely the brake will soon be back out of adjustment since this procedure usually does not fix the underlying adjustment problem.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 5, Air Brakes, Subsection 5.3.2, Walk-around Inspection, Slack Adjusters

topic: Inspecting Air Brake Systems - Brake Drums, Linings, and Hoses
question: What is the limit on crack length in a brake drum or disc during inspection?
choice_a: Cracks are never acceptable, of any length
choice_b: Cracks up to two-thirds the width of the friction area are acceptable
choice_c: Any crack under three inches is acceptable
choice_d: Cracks must not be longer than one half the width of the friction area
explanation: Brake drums (or discs) must not have cracks longer than one half the width of the friction area.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 5, Air Brakes, Subsection 5.3.2, Walk-around Inspection, Brake Drums, Linings, and Hoses

topic: Inspecting Air Brake Systems - Brake Drums, Linings, and Hoses
question: What condition must brake linings (friction material) NOT be in, according to the inspection checklist?
choice_a: Painted any color other than black
choice_b: Cooler than the drum
choice_c: Attached with rivets rather than bolts
choice_d: Loose, soaked with oil or grease, or dangerously thin
explanation: Linings (friction material) must not be loose or soaked with oil or grease, and must not be dangerously thin; mechanical parts must be in place, not broken or missing.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 5, Air Brakes, Subsection 5.3.2, Walk-around Inspection, Brake Drums, Linings, and Hoses

topic: Inspecting Air Brake Systems - Brake Drums, Linings, and Hoses
question: What should a driver check regarding the air hoses connected to the brake chambers?
choice_a: That they are painted the correct color
choice_b: That they match the alcohol evaporator hose diameter
choice_c: That they aren't cut or worn due to rubbing
choice_d: That they are longer than the wheelbase
explanation: Check the air hoses connected to the brake chambers to make sure they aren't cut or worn due to rubbing.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 5, Air Brakes, Subsection 5.3.2, Walk-around Inspection, Brake Drums, Linings, and Hoses

topic: Final Air Brake Check - Governor Cut-in and Cut-out
question: During the final air brake check, pumping by the air compressor should start at about what pressure and stop at about what pressure?
choice_a: Start at about 100 psi, stop at about 125 psi
choice_b: Start at about 125 psi, stop at about 150 psi
choice_c: Start at about 55 psi, stop at about 100 psi
choice_d: Start at about 20 psi, stop at about 45 psi
explanation: Pumping by the air compressor should start (cut-in) at about 100 psi and stop (cut-out) at about 125 psi; the driver should check the manufacturer's specifications.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 5, Air Brakes, Subsection 5.3.3, Step 7 Final Air Brake Check, Check Air Compressor Governor Cut-in and Cut-out Pressures

topic: Final Air Brake Check - Governor Cut-in and Cut-out
question: What could happen if the air governor does not cut in and cut out as described?
choice_a: Nothing, the governor is purely cosmetic
choice_b: A governor that does not work properly may not keep enough air pressure for safe driving
choice_c: It only affects fuel economy
choice_d: It automatically triggers the ABS malfunction lamp
explanation: If the air governor does not work as described, it may need to be fixed; a governor that does not work properly may not keep enough air pressure for safe driving.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 5, Air Brakes, Subsection 5.3.3, Step 7 Final Air Brake Check, Check Air Compressor Governor Cut-in and Cut-out Pressures

topic: Final Air Brake Check - Air Leakage Rate
question: With a fully-charged single vehicle air system, engine off and parking brake released, the air pressure loss rate should be less than what amount in one minute?
choice_a: Four psi
choice_b: Three psi
choice_c: One psi
choice_d: Two psi
explanation: With a fully-charged air system (typically 125 psi), engine off, and parking brake released, the loss rate should be less than two psi in one minute for single vehicles.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 5, Air Brakes, Subsection 5.3.3, Step 7 Final Air Brake Check, Test Air Leakage Rate

topic: Final Air Brake Check - Air Leakage Rate
question: For a combination vehicle under the same fully-charged, engine-off leakage test, what is the maximum acceptable air pressure loss rate in one minute?
choice_a: Less than three psi
choice_b: Less than five psi
choice_c: Less than two psi
choice_d: Less than four psi
explanation: The loss rate should be less than two psi in one minute for single vehicles and less than three psi in one minute for combination vehicles.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 5, Air Brakes, Subsection 5.3.3, Step 7 Final Air Brake Check, Test Air Leakage Rate

topic: Final Air Brake Check - Brake Application Air Loss
question: With air pressure built up to governor cutoff and the foot brake fully applied and held for one minute, how much air pressure drop is acceptable for a single vehicle?
choice_a: No more than three pounds
choice_b: No more than eight pounds
choice_c: No more than one pound
choice_d: No more than four pounds
explanation: With the air pressure built up to governor cutoff (120-140 psi), the foot brake fully applied and held for one minute, the air pressure should not drop more than three pounds in one minute for a single vehicle.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 5, Air Brakes, Subsection 5.3.3, Step 7 Final Air Brake Check, Check Air Compressor Governor Cut-in and Cut-out Pressures

topic: Final Air Brake Check - Brake Application Air Loss
question: In the same foot-brake-held test, how many pounds of pressure drop in one minute is acceptable for a combination vehicle?
choice_a: Three pounds
choice_b: Four pounds
choice_c: Five pounds
choice_d: Two pounds
explanation: The air pressure should not drop more than three pounds in one minute for a single vehicle, or four pounds in one minute for a combination vehicle; if the loss is greater, the driver should check for air leaks and fix them before driving.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 5, Air Brakes, Subsection 5.3.3, Step 7 Final Air Brake Check, Check Air Compressor Governor Cut-in and Cut-out Pressures

topic: Final Air Brake Check - Low Pressure Warning Signal Test
question: During the final air brake check, the low air pressure warning signal must come on before the pressure drops below what level in the tank with the lowest pressure?
choice_a: 35 psi
choice_b: 55 psi
choice_c: 65 psi
choice_d: 45 psi
explanation: The low air pressure warning signal must come on before the pressure drops to less than 55 psi in the air tank, or the tank with the lowest air pressure in dual air systems.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 5, Air Brakes, Subsection 5.3.3, Step 7 Final Air Brake Check, Test Low Pressure Warning Signal

topic: Final Air Brake Check - Low Pressure Warning Signal Test
question: What could happen in a single-circuit air system if the low air pressure warning signal doesn't work?
choice_a: It could cause sudden emergency braking because the driver would lose air pressure without knowing it
choice_b: It would only affect the brake lights
choice_c: The spring brakes would never engage
choice_d: Nothing, the compressor compensates automatically
explanation: If the warning signal doesn't work, you could lose air pressure and not know it, which could cause sudden emergency braking in a single-circuit air system; in dual systems the stopping distance would be increased instead.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 5, Air Brakes, Subsection 5.3.3, Step 7 Final Air Brake Check, Test Low Pressure Warning Signal

topic: Final Air Brake Check - Spring Brakes Coming On Automatically
question: On a tractor-trailer combination, what should happen to the tractor protection valve and parking brake valve as air pressure is fanned down to the manufacturer's specification?
choice_a: They should trigger the ABS malfunction lamp
choice_b: They should open wider to allow more airflow
choice_c: They should close (pop out), causing the spring brakes to come on
choice_d: They should remain unaffected until the engine is restarted
explanation: The tractor protection valve and parking brake valve should close (pop out) on a tractor-trailer combination vehicle when the air pressure falls to the manufacturer's specification (20-45 psi), causing the spring brakes to come on.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 5, Air Brakes, Subsection 5.3.3, Step 7 Final Air Brake Check, Check That Spring Brakes Come On Automatically

topic: Final Air Brake Check - Rate of Air Pressure Buildup
question: In a dual air system, with the engine at operating rpms, pressure should build from 85 to 100 psi within approximately what time?
choice_a: 3 minutes
choice_b: 45 seconds
choice_c: 30 seconds
choice_d: 15 seconds
explanation: When the engine is at operating rpms, the pressure should build from 85 to 100 psi within 45 seconds in dual air systems.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 5, Air Brakes, Subsection 5.3.3, Step 7 Final Air Brake Check, Check Rate of Air Pressure Buildup

topic: Final Air Brake Check - Rate of Air Pressure Buildup
question: In a single air system on a pre-1975 vehicle, what is a typical requirement for pressure buildup, and at what idle speed?
choice_a: Buildup from 85 to 100 psi within 45 seconds at any idle speed
choice_b: Buildup from 20 to 45 psi within 1 minute
choice_c: Buildup from 100 to 125 psi within 10 seconds
choice_d: Buildup from 50 to 90 psi within 3 minutes with the engine at an idle speed of 600-900 rpm
explanation: In single air systems (pre-1975), typical requirements are pressure build-up from 50 to 90 psi within 3 minutes with the engine at an idle speed of 600-900 rpms.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 5, Air Brakes, Subsection 5.3.3, Step 7 Final Air Brake Check, Check Rate of Air Pressure Buildup

topic: Final Air Brake Check - Rate of Air Pressure Buildup
question: What could happen if air pressure does not build up fast enough during the buildup test?
choice_a: It automatically triggers a recall notice
choice_b: Nothing of concern, this is normal on cold days
choice_c: It only affects the alcohol evaporator
choice_d: The driver's pressure may drop too low during driving, requiring an emergency stop; the vehicle should not be driven until fixed
explanation: If air pressure does not build up fast enough, pressure may drop too low during driving, requiring an emergency stop; the driver should not drive until the problem is fixed.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 5, Air Brakes, Subsection 5.3.3, Step 7 Final Air Brake Check, Check Rate of Air Pressure Buildup

topic: Final Air Brake Check - Test Parking Brake
question: How should a driver test the parking brake as part of the final air brake check?
choice_a: Only inspect the knob visually
choice_b: Drive at highway speed and pull the knob suddenly
choice_c: Stop the vehicle, apply the parking brake, and gently pull against it in a low gear to see that it holds
choice_d: Release the parking brake and coast downhill
explanation: To test the parking brake, stop the vehicle, put the parking brake on, and gently pull against it in a low gear to test that the parking brake will hold.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 5, Air Brakes, Subsection 5.3.3, Step 7 Final Air Brake Check, Test Parking Brake

topic: Final Air Brake Check - Test Service Brakes
question: How should a driver test the service brakes as part of the final air brake check?
choice_a: Move the vehicle forward slowly (about five mph) and apply the brakes firmly, noting any pulling, unusual feel, or delayed stopping
choice_b: Only inspect the brakes visually without moving the vehicle
choice_c: Test only at highway speed with a hard stop
choice_d: Use only the parking brake control for this test
explanation: To test service brakes, wait for normal air pressure, release the parking brake, move the vehicle forward slowly (about five mph), and apply the brakes firmly using the brake pedal, noting any vehicle pulling, unusual feel, or delayed stopping action.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 5, Air Brakes, Subsection 5.3.3, Step 7 Final Air Brake Check, Test Service Brakes

question: In a vehicle with a manual transmission, when should the driver push the clutch in during a normal stop?
choice_a: Only after the vehicle has come to a complete stop
choice_b: The clutch should never be used when braking
choice_c: Not until the engine rpm is down close to idle
choice_d: Immediately after pushing the brake pedal
explanation: If you have a manual transmission, don't push the clutch in until the engine rpm is down close to idle; when stopped, select a starting gear.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 5, Air Brakes, Subsection 5.4.1, Normal Stops

question: What can happen if a driver brakes hard on slippery surfaces in a vehicle without ABS?
choice_a: The alcohol evaporator activates
choice_b: The wheels may lock up, causing loss of steering control if steering wheels lock, or skidding, jackknifing, or spinning if other wheels lock
choice_c: The spring brakes engage automatically
choice_d: Nothing unusual happens
explanation: When you brake hard on slippery surfaces in a vehicle without ABS, your wheels may lock up; when steering wheels lock up you lose steering control, and when other wheels lock up you may skid, jackknife, or even spin the vehicle.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 5, Air Brakes, Subsection 5.4.2, Braking with Antilock Brakes

question: How does ABS help a driver avoid wheel lockup?
choice_a: It shifts braking load to the parking brake
choice_b: The computer senses impending lockup and reduces braking pressure to a safe level so the driver maintains control
choice_c: It increases pressure to all wheels equally at all times
choice_d: It disables the front brakes entirely
explanation: ABS helps you avoid wheel lock up; the computer senses impending lockup, reduces the braking pressure to a safe level, and you maintain control.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 5, Air Brakes, Subsection 5.4.2, Braking with Antilock Brakes

question: If only the tractor has ABS in a combination vehicle, what should the driver watch for?
choice_a: Nothing different from normal driving
choice_b: The alcohol evaporator level
choice_c: The trailer, letting up on the brakes (if safe) if it begins to swing out
choice_d: The front brake limiting valve position
explanation: When only the tractor has ABS, the driver should be able to maintain steering control with less chance of jackknifing, but should keep an eye on the trailer and let up on the brakes, if it can be done safely, if the trailer begins to swing out.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 5, Air Brakes, Subsection 5.4.2, Braking with Antilock Brakes

question: According to the manual, what is the one exception in which a driver may fully apply the brakes in an emergency stop even though ABS guidance is normally to brake as usual?
choice_a: Only bobtail tractors
choice_b: Driving a straight truck or combination with working ABS on all axles
choice_c: Any vehicle with ABS on only the trailer
choice_d: Any vehicle regardless of ABS status, in all emergencies
explanation: There is only one exception to braking the same way regardless of ABS location: if you always drive a straight truck or combination with working ABS on all axles, in an emergency stop you can fully apply the brakes.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 5, Air Brakes, Subsection 5.4.2, Braking with Antilock Brakes

question: What should a driver do if their ABS malfunctions?
choice_a: Disconnect the service brakes
choice_b: Increase speed to compensate
choice_c: Stop driving immediately and never move the vehicle again
